summary: Proposes a way to carry any protocol over a CLNS network using Generic Routing Encapsulation, which can be used to tunnel IPv4 or IPv6 across CLNS.

eli5.summary: It puts one kind of package inside another kind to ship it across a road that only takes the second kind.

questions: how do you tunnel ip over clns
how do sonet networks migrate to ip
subtitle: How to wrap IP packets inside CLNS for migration from old networks to new.

tldr.problem: Large SONET and SDH management networks are built on CLNS, but newer IP-based equipment needs to be installed on networks that still use CLNS. There was no standard method to tunnel IP over CLNS.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes using GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation, from RFC 2784) as a tunnel protocol. A GRE packet is wrapped inside a CLNS data payload, and the N-SEL (NSAP selector) byte is set to 47 to identify GRE traffic.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can now migrate from CLNS to IP gradually, with new IP equipment coexisting alongside old CLNS equipment by using standardized GRE tunneling.

today: RFC 3147 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. While the industry has largely completed its transition from CLNS to IP, this RFC remains a reference for legacy network operations and migration scenarios involving SONET/SDH management networks.

sections.title: Tunneling IP Over Legacy Networks
sections.content:
This RFC addresses a migration challenge: large networks used for managing SONET (Synchronous Optical Network) and SDH (Synchronous Digital Hierarchy) equipment are mandated by standards (Bellcore GR-253-CORE and ITU-T G.784) to use CLNS (Connectionless Network Service). However, vendors are now offering IP-based management interfaces, and a migration path is needed.

The RFC acknowledges that RFC 2784 (GRE) and RFC 1702 already enable tunneling CLNS over IP, but no standard existed for the reverse: tunneling IP over CLNS. GRE is an ideal choice because it is generic, already in use in the reverse direction, and supports any protocol with an Ethernet Protocol Type.
sections.eli5: Old phone networks use a language called CLNS. New equipment speaks IP. We need a way for them to understand each other while everything is changing.

sections.title: How GRE Over CLNS Works
sections.content:
A GRE packet (which includes the GRE header plus an encapsulated IP payload) is placed inside the data portion of a CLNS Data Type PDU (DT PDU). The CLNS PDU structure includes a Network Layer Protocol Identifier, addressing information, and a data field; the GRE packet occupies the data field entirely.

The CLNS stack at the receiving end reads the N-SEL byte from the destination address to determine that the payload is GRE, then passes the GRE packet to the GRE decoder. The GRE decoder inspects the GRE Protocol Type field to learn whether the encapsulated packet is IPv4, IPv6, or another protocol.

The overhead of this approach is minimal: GRE adds only 4 bytes (2 flag/version bytes plus 2 protocol-type bytes) to each IP packet. Given the large size of CLNS headers, this is negligible.
sections.eli5: GRE is a wrapper. You put your IP packet in the wrapper and drop it into a CLNS package. When it arrives, the receiver unwraps it layer by layer.

sections.title: Configuration and Parameters
sections.content:
The N-SEL (NSAP Selector) value is used to identify the type of payload, similar to how the IP Protocol Type field works in IPv4. The RFC recommends using N-SEL value 47 (decimal) in both the source and destination addresses of the CLNP PDU to indicate GRE. The value 47 is chosen because it is the IP protocol number for GRE (from RFC 1700) and is not commonly used as an N-SEL value in existing networks.

The Segmentation Permitted (SP) flag should be set in all CLNP PDUs containing GRE packets. If SP is not set and a PDU exceeds a link's MTU, the packet is dropped with no indication to the sender, potentially forming a black hole. With SP set, the network can fragment the PDU instead.
sections.eli5: N-SEL 47 is the label that says 'this is GRE inside.' The SP flag tells the network it is okay to split big packages into smaller ones.

sections.title: MTU and Path Discovery
sections.content:
When a tunnel entry point receives an IP packet destined for the tunnel, it must respect Path MTU Discovery (PMTU, from RFC 1191). If the IP packet is larger than the GRE tunnel's MTU and the packet's Don't Fragment (DF) bit is not set, the tunnel entry point must fragment it before wrapping it in GRE.

If the packet has DF set and is too large for the tunnel, the entry point discards it and sends back an ICMP unreachable message with code fragmentation needed and DF set. This signals the original sender to use smaller packets. This behavior ensures that PMTU discovery works correctly through the GRE tunnel.
sections.eli5: Big packages might not fit through the tunnel. If they cannot be split, the sender gets a message: 'make smaller packages.'

sections.title: No Native Security
sections.content:
Neither CLNS nor GRE provides any encryption or authentication on their own. The RFC states plainly: CLNS and GRE do not provide any security when employed in the way recommended in this document.

If security is needed, it must be provided by other methods applied to the payload before it enters the tunnel. For example, using IPsec (IP Security) to encrypt the IP payload before it is wrapped in GRE, or applying TLS/SSL at the application layer. This separation of concerns allows network operators to choose security mechanisms independently of the tunneling protocol.
sections.eli5: GRE and CLNS do not lock the package. If you need a lock, add it yourself before wrapping.
